mainTopic: Declaring a field הפקר for a limited time, and whether the ברייתא follows רבנן or רבי יוסי
overview: The גמרא quotes the end (סיפא) of a ברייתא about someone who makes his field הפקר for a set time, such as a day, a year or a seven-year cycle. That end lets him retract until someone takes the field, which sounds like רבי יוסי, who ties הפקר to someone taking the item. But the first part (רישא) of the same ברייתא seemed to follow רבנן. עולא answers that both parts follow רבנן, and that a time-limited הפקר is an unusual case where even רבנן let the owner retract. ריש לקיש answers the opposite way: both parts follow רבי יוסי, and the רישא's three-day rule is a safeguard made by חכמים so the laws of הפקר are not forgotten. רבה explains that חכמים did not make it final from the first day because of swindlers who declare הפקר and then take it back. The גמרא then asks what the item's status is by Torah law, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A field made ownerless for a limited time
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that someone who makes his field הפקר for a set time can take it back as long as nobody has taken it. Once someone has taken it, he cannot take it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person says, 'This field is ownerless for a day, a week, a month, a year, or a seven-year cycle,' then as long as nobody (neither he nor anyone else) has taken it, he can change his mind. Once someone (he or anyone else) has taken it, he can no longer change his mind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last part (the סיפא) of a ברייתא it has been discussing. This sets up a problem that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the key moment is when someone takes the field (זכיה). Before that, the owner can still back out. After that, he cannot. Making the taking the deciding moment sounds like the view of רבי יוסי.

keyTerms.meaning: Ownerless property that anyone may take
Took possession of it, acquired it
To retract, to change one's mind
Here: a seven-year cycle (a 'week of years')

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר ״תְּהֵא שָׂדֶה זוֹ מוּפְקֶרֶת לְיוֹם אֶחָד״,
phrases.english: If one said: 'This field will be ownerless for one day,'
'for one week,' 'for one month,'
phrases.notes: Here שבת means a week, not the day of rest.

phrases.english: 'for one year,' 'for one seven-year cycle,'
as long as no one took possession of it,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין הוּא בֵּין אַחֵר יָכוֹל לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ.
phrases.english: neither he nor another, he is able to retract.
Once one took possession of it,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין הוּא בֵּין אַחֵר, אֵין יָכוֹל לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ.
phrases.english: whether he or another, he is unable to retract.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר תְּהֵא שָׂדֶה זוֹ מוּפְקֶרֶת לְיוֹם אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא that the סוגיא was already discussing; this is its closing clause.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a time-limited הפקר, the owner can retract until someone takes possession, but not after.

steps.title: The two halves of the ברייתא seem to follow different opinions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the first part of the ברייתא fits רבנן, while the last part fits רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first part follows the רבנן, and the last part follows רבי יוסי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a problem: one ברייתא seems to be split between two opposing opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רישא, quoted earlier, has the הפקר take hold even when nobody took the item, which fits רבנן. The סיפא makes taking possession the deciding point, which fits רבי יוסי. A single ברייתא should not switch opinions halfway through.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of a teaching
The last clause of a teaching

steps.confusionAlert: The רישא is the earlier part of the ברייתא, quoted before this section. It is not the part quoted in step 1. Step 1 is the סיפא.

phrases.english: The first clause follows the Rabbis,
and the latter clause follows Rabbi Yosei!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ברייתא just quoted by comparing it with its own first clause.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רישא lets הפקר take hold without anyone taking the item (like רבנן). The סיפא depends on taking possession (like רבי יוסי). So the ברייתא contradicts itself.

steps.title: עולא: the last part also follows רבנן
steps.stepSummary: עולא answers that the סיפא also follows רבנן, so the whole ברייתא is consistent.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: The last part is also the view of the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא solves the problem by saying the whole ברייתא follows רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both parts follow רבנן, there is no split. But this leaves a question: why would רבנן ever let the owner take back his הפקר? The next step asks exactly that.

phrases.english: Ulla said:
The latter clause is also the Rabbis.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר עוּלָּא סֵיפָא נָמֵי רַבָּנַן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the סיפא to the same opinion as the רישא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two halves follow different opinions.

steps.title: But רבנן don't allow taking back הפקר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges עולא: if this follows רבנן, why can the owner retract before anyone takes the field?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does it say that as long as nobody (he or anyone else) took it, he can change his mind?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on עולא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבנן, whether הפקר takes hold does not depend on anyone taking the item. So the סיפא's rule, which makes retracting depend on whether someone took it, does not seem to fit רבנן.

phrases.english: If so,
why is it that as long as no one took possession of it,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין הוּא בֵּין אַחֵר, יָכוֹל לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ?
phrases.english: neither he nor another, he is able to retract?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי אַמַּאי עַד שֶׁלֹּא זָכָה בָּהּ
steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's claim that the סיפא follows רבנן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For רבנן, הפקר does not depend on anyone taking the item, yet the סיפא lets the owner retract only until someone takes it.

steps.title: Time-limited הפקר is unusual and different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that making something הפקר for a year or a seven-year cycle is unusual, so even רבנן treat it differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: A year or a seven-year cycle is different, because such cases are not common.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends עולא by calling time-limited הפקר a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, הפקר is meant to be permanent. Giving something up for only a set time is unusual. It shows the owner kept some rights for himself, so even רבנן let him retract before anyone takes it. The basic category of הפקר still applies; only this unusual case has a different outcome.
steps.whatToRemember: עולא's approach: the whole ברייתא follows רבנן, and a time-limited הפקר is an unusual exception where the owner can still retract.

phrases.english: A year and a seven-year cycle are different,
since they are not common.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4 and completes עולא's approach.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the case as an unusual exception
steps.terutzHavaAmina: For רבנן, the right to retract never depends on someone taking the item.
steps.terutzMaskana: In an unusual time-limited הפקר, even רבנן allow retracting before anyone takes it.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: the first part also follows רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש answers the opposite way: the whole ברייתא follows רבי יוסי, and the רישא's rule is a rabbinic safeguard so people don't forget how הפקר works.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: Since the last part is רבי יוסי, the first part is also רבי יוסי. The reason for the first part is so that the laws of הפקר will not be forgotten.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives a different answer to the problem from step 2. He says both parts follow רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By רבי יוסי's basic rule, the owner could always retract before anyone takes the item. So the רישא's rule, where the הפקר takes hold without anyone taking it, must be an extra rule made by חכמים. They made it so people would not lose track of how הפקר works and wrongly think it can always be undone.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common move in the גמרא: a rule that seems to fit another opinion is explained as a rabbinic safeguard added on top of the basic law.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
Since the latter clause is Rabbi Yosei,
the first clause is also Rabbi Yosei.
And in the first clause, this is the reason:
so that the laws of ownerlessness will not be forgotten.

steps.triggerLanguage: רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר מִדְּסֵיפָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי רֵישָׁא נָמֵי רַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the contradiction of step 2 and offers an approach opposite to עולא's.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the רישא to רבי יוסי and explains it as a rabbinic safeguard
steps.terutzMaskana: The רישא follows רבי יוסי, and its rule is a rabbinic safeguard.

steps.title: Then why not make it final from the first day?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if חכמים added a safeguard, why not make the הפקר final starting on day one?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, it should be ownerless even from the first day!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the goal is to protect the laws of הפקר, the strongest safeguard would make it final right away. So why did חכמים give the owner a three-day window to retract?

phrases.english: If so, even from the first day
let it also be ownerless!
phrases.notes: He means: let it become final with no chance to take it back, starting from day one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי אֲפִילּוּ מִיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן נָמֵי לֶיהֱוֵי הֶפְקֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges ריש לקיש's safeguard explanation from step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The three-day timing of the rabbinic safeguard
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the safeguard is meant to protect the laws of הפקר, it should start immediately, not after three days.

steps.title: רבה: because of swindlers
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that חכמים did not make it final from day one because of swindlers, who would declare הפקר and then take it right back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Because of the swindlers, who declare things ownerless and then take them back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers the challenge and closes ריש לקיש's approach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some cheaters would declare a field הפקר for a moment and then grab it back, so its produce would count as הפקר and be free of מעשרות. If it became final right away, this trick would work cleanly. Delaying the result discourages this abuse.

keyTerms.meaning: They go back on them, take them back

steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש's approach: the whole ברייתא follows רבי יוסי. The three-day rule is a rabbinic safeguard so the laws of הפקר are not forgotten, and it is delayed because of swindlers.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
Because of the swindlers,
who declare things ownerless and then take them back.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a practical reason for the delay
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The safeguard should apply from the first day.
steps.terutzMaskana: The safeguard is delayed to stop swindlers from abusing הפקר.

steps.title: What is the item's status by Torah law?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether, by Torah law, the item is not truly הפקר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But by Torah law, is it not הפקר?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short follow-up question about the rabbinic rule it just explained. It is setting up the next move, where it will clarify what the Torah itself says about this הפקר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 6 and 8 said the three-day rule was made by חכמים. That raises a question about the Torah level. If the item became final only because חכמים said so, does the Torah by itself not treat it as הפקר? The גמרא wants to pin down the Torah-level status before going further.

keyTerms.meaning: By Torah law (as opposed to a rule made by חכמים)
Ownerless property that anyone may take
Is not, does not count as

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new argument against ריש לקיש. It is a quick question about Torah law that follows from his rabbinic-safeguard answer.

phrases.english: But by Torah law,
is it not ownerless?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from ריש לקיש's answer in step 6 and רבה's explanation in step 8. Both said the time limit is rabbinic, so the גמרא asks what the Torah-level status is.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether, by Torah law and according to רבי יוסי, the declared item counts as הפקר, apart from the safeguard חכמים added.
